11:
⚠ Changing the baud rate makes this tool lose contact with the module immediately (manual: effective right after OK)!
Recovery: 1) Disconnect  2) Change the baud rate dropdown above to the new value  3) Reconnect (this power-cycles the module)  4) Re-run the power-on ritual (RTS/DTR).
The trailing ;&W stores the new baud rate in NV — drop it and the module reverts on reboot, leaving you disconnected twice over.

19: URC = Unsolicited Result Code: a message the module emits on its own, not a reply to any command — RDY / +CPIN: READY at power-on, SMS arrival, incoming TCP data and Wi-Fi scan results are all URCs. This group controls the URC output port and the master switch; if the output port is not uart1, this tool (which runs over UART) will never see a single URC.

68: Network info: access technology / operator code / band / channel
70: Makes the module report quality data on its own whenever the signal changes, so you do not have to hammer AT+CSQ. The RSRP / RSRQ / SINR from SQI are the three metrics that actually define LTE quality — AT+CSQ only gives a coarse RSSI (and BER is stuck at 99 on this unit, so it tells you nothing). Antenna and placement testing is impossible without this group. Reading them: RSRP = signal strength, RSRQ = quality, SINR = signal-to-noise ratio (higher is better; low means interference). ⚠ It only pushes when the signal actually changes — sitting still can mean long silence, so cup the antenna in your hand or unplug and replug it to force a change. The setting does not survive a reboot; enable it again every time.
71: Query the current sqi reporting switch (no value = query; "csq" / "all" work the same way)
72: Enable active RSRP/RSRQ/SINR reporting — no other command gives you these three values, and antenna and placement testing needs them
73: Reports as soon as the signal changes, replacing repeated AT+CSQ presses
74: One-click mute (for when URCs flood the terminal) — remember to turn it back on afterwards
75: Disables all URC reporting: every event notification from GNSS / TCP-IP / MQTT / Wi-Fi Scan goes silent.
78: A PDP context is the "data channel" the carrier allocates; without one there is no usable IP. This group is read-only queries at the 3GPP standard layer, which is NOT the same layer as QIACT? / QICSGP on the TCP/IP page — those belong to Quectel's own protocol stack. The two layers can disagree, and comparing them side by side tells you whether the fault is on the network side or the module side: an IP here but none on the TCP/IP page means the network granted one but the stack never started. This unit activates context 1 and gets an IP automatically at power-on (measured), so manual intervention is normally unnecessary.
79: Defined PDP contexts and APNs (one line per context)
80: Activation state of each context (the response is cid,state; note that the write form takes them in the opposite order)
82: The IP each context actually obtained — an IP at the 3GPP layer does not mean the Quectel stack is up
83: Cumulative bytes sent/received (accumulates across reboots; useful for metering a roaming SIM)
85: Detailed cause of the last failure (covers attach and PDP activation failures) — a different layer from QIGETERROR on the TCP/IP page
87: Controls the radio and the network attach — everything here changes module state (every red-framed button asks again before acting). CFUN levels: 1 = full functionality, 4 = airplane (TX/RX off, SIM still alive), 0 = minimum (SIM disabled too), 1,1 = soft-reset the whole module. Recovery is always AT+CFUN=1; ⚠ if the SIM has a PIN lock you must re-enter the PIN after going back to 1 before it registers. CGATT is the PS domain attach switch, and detaching kills every TCP/MQTT connection. Commands here can block for 15 to 140 s — wait patiently after pressing, do not mash the button.
88: Query the current functionality level: 1=full, 0=minimum, 4=RF off — check this before pressing the set buttons below
90: Restore full functionality (radio fully on) — use this to recover after turning the radio off
91: Re-enables the radio and re-scans and re-attaches, which may interrupt a TCP / MQTT test in progress.
92: Airplane mode (TX and RX off) — the starting point for testing the re-entry-to-network flow
93: Turns the radio off: drops off the network immediately and kills every PDP and socket. Recover with AT+CFUN=1.
94: Minimum functionality (the manual only says "Minimum functionality" and never states which subsystems it turns off)
95: Minimum functionality mode: drops off the network and disables the SIM as well (AT+CPIN? returns +CME ERROR: 13). Recover with AT+CFUN=1.
96: Soft-reset the module (<rst>=1 is only allowed with <fun>=1)
97: ⚠ Soft-resets the whole module! The AT port goes dead briefly and you have to wait for RDY again. Every connection and unsaved setting is lost.
98: Trigger a PS attach manually (pair it with AT+CEER to find the cause when it fails)
99: Attaches to the PS domain; may block for up to 140 s.
100: Detach from the PS domain manually — for testing the re-attach flow
101: ⚠ Breaks the data bearer: sockets opened on the TCP/IP page and connections on the MQTT page all go down with it. Blocks for up to 140 s.

130: Fix acceleration (shorter TTFF): AP-Flash stores the ephemeris in flash, so a re-power within an hour becomes a fast hot start (on from the factory on this unit); AGNSS downloads assistance data from the network when GNSS starts, cutting a cold start down to seconds or minutes (needs a PDP, costs data, takes effect after a reboot).
131: Query the current AP-Flash fast-hot-start value (measured factory value on this unit: 1 = on)
132: Enable: the ephemeris is stored in flash and imported at the next power-on (valid 1 hour, refreshed automatically every hour); effective immediately, written to NVRAM

134: Query the AGNSS network-assisted positioning status (measured factory value on this unit: 0 = disabled)
135: Enable AGNSS — cuts a cold start down to seconds or minutes; takes effect after a reboot, written to NVRAM
136: Once enabled (a reboot is required), every GNSS start downloads assistance data from the network: it needs an active PDP context and consumes data (billed on the 1NCE roaming SIM, roughly tens of KB per run).
137: Disable AGNSS (takes effect after a reboot)
138: Query the AGNSS server setting (measured factory value: asrmicro allstar; only change it if the server changes)
140: Activates the data channel of the Quectel protocol stack — TCP / SSL / HTTP / FTP / MQTT all need it first. Flow: "Act PDP" to activate, then "Query IP" to confirm you got an IP. ⚠ This SIM allows only one PDP, and the network already activates one at power-on (the ID varies) — if Act PDP returns ERROR (QIGETERROR 572), go to the Network page, find that ID with AT+CGACT?, free the slot with AT+CGACT=0,<id>, then come back and activate. The APN syncs automatically at power-on, so setting it by hand is usually unnecessary.
141: Activate PDP context 1 (dial up the data connection); waits up to 150 s and no other command should be issued meanwhile; starts generating data traffic (mind roaming charges)
142: Query the activated contexts and the local IP obtained (returns just OK before activation)
143: Set context 1's APN manually (IPv4 / PAP are fixed) — normally unnecessary, it syncs automatically at power-on
144:
⚠ You normally do NOT need this button — at power-on the module syncs its APN from the PDP definition the network hands down
(measured on this SIM: iot.1nce.net right after boot), so AT+QIACT=1 alone gets you an IP.

Set it by hand only when the APN is not handed down automatically (for example a corporate APN that needs a username and password).
A wrong APN makes QIACT fail; the setting is not stored and is lost when the module reboots.

147: This unit's SIM (1NCE IoT card) — the value measured as handed down automatically at power-on
148: The generic APN for most Taiwanese carriers
150: PPP dial-up username; leave it empty for most Taiwanese carriers
153: PPP dial-up password; leave it empty for most Taiwanese carriers
154: Deactivate context 1 and force-close every connection under it (up to 40 s)

163: The domain name to resolve to an IP (on 2026-08-06 the user switched this to google — globally resolvable and it returns several A records, a better test baseline than the original quectel.com)

183: Query the total received / read / unread data lengths
186: Query client 0's MQTT protocol version (no value = query)
190: How long without data before a PING keeps the connection alive; range 0-3600, default 120, 0=disabled

195: The MQTT broker's domain name or IP
198: MQTT port; normally 1883 for plaintext and 8883 for TLS
199: Query the MQTT network that is open
200: Connect to the broker (append ,"user","pass" yourself if credentials are needed); success URC +QMTCONN: 0,0,0

206: Subscribe to a topic (msgid fixed at 1); incoming messages are then reported as URC +QMTRECV

213: The MQTT topic to publish to
216: Manual: it may be 0 only when qos=0; with qos=1 or 2 it must be 1-65535

219: Unsubscribe from a topic (msgid fixed at 2)

222: Go offline from the broker (sends MQTT DISCONNECT)
223: Close the MQTT network (unnecessary after a normal QMTDISC)
225: Query support and parameter ranges (measured as supported on this unit)
227: Read the current scan parameters (measured default on this unit: 12000,1,5,5,0)

229: Scan with custom parameters; results arrive asynchronously after OK, up to 13 s
231: Time limit for a single scan, range 4000-255000, default 12000
233: How many rounds to scan. **The measured range on this unit is 1-3** (actual AT+QWIFISCAN=? reply on 2026-08-06; the earlier 1-6 taken from the application note was wrong), default 1; duplicate MACs are removed across rounds
235: How many access points to report at most. **The measured range on this unit is 4-10** (actual reply on 2026-08-06; the earlier 4-30 taken from the application note was wrong), default 5; the scan ends early once the quota is filled. Raise it to see everything where there are many APs
237: RRC polling timeout, range 0-255 s, default 5
239: 0=data service first, 1=Wi-Fi scan first (may interrupt cellular data)
240: Query every SSL configuration sub-item and parameter range
241: Set the protocol version of SSL context 1
243: 0=SSL 3.0, 1=TLS 1.0, 2=TLS 1.1, 3=TLS 1.2, 4=all supported. 4 gives the best compatibility (the server picks). Manual §1.2 lists SSL 3.0 / TLS 1.0 / 1.1 / 1.2 as supported and does not list TLS 1.3; the manual states no factory default.
244: Query the current protocol version of SSL context 1
245: Set the cipher suite; 0XFFFF = all supported
247: Hexadecimal format. 0XFFFF = every suite in the table above (manual: all suites are enabled by default). Common single codes: 0X0035=TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA, 0X002F=TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, 0X003D=TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256, 0XC013=TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, 0XC02F=TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, 0XC030=ECDHE_RSA_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. Manual §1.2 lists 33 of them in total.
248: Set the authentication mode; the default 0 = no certificate verification, and it is the only path this tool can complete
250: 0=no verification at all; 1=verify the server (a trusted CA certificate must already be in the module's UFS); 2=mutual server plus client verification (a client cert and private key are also needed when the peer asks for them). Manual §4 says it plainly: with seclevel 1 or 2 you must first upload the certificate with AT+QFUPL — this tool cannot send binary files, so 1 or 2 will always fail the handshake (unless someone else's certificate is already in the module).
251: Query the current certificate authentication mode
252: Query the configured CA certificate path (read-only)
253: Specify the CA certificate path (the file must already be in UFS)
255: Manual §3.2 uses UFS:cacert.pem as its example. This only points at the file; the file itself must have been uploaded to the module's UFS with AT+QFUPL beforehand — which this tool cannot do. It is only meaningful when that file already exists in the module (uploaded by someone else with another tool).
256: SNI: turn it on for virtual hosts and CDNs
258: 0=disabled, 1=enabled. SNI puts the host name into the Client Hello as an extension so several virtual servers on one IP can pick the right certificate (manual §1.6). TLS only. Sites behind a CDN or on a shared IP usually require it, otherwise the peer returns the wrong certificate.
259: Whether to skip the certificate validity period check
261: 0=do not skip (the module compares its local time against the certificate's Not before / Not after, so a wrong clock makes the certificate look expired), 1=skip. Manual §1.5: to run the validity check you must first set the module's time inside the certificate's validity window with AT+CCLK. With seclevel=0 no certificate is verified at all, so this item does nothing.
262: Maximum TLS handshake wait in seconds (10-300)
264: Range 10–300 s, manual default 300. This value is ADDED to the maximum response time of QSSLOPEN (150 s for the network plus this value), so a small value during testing shows you the failure sooner instead of waiting out 450 s.
265: Query the current handshake timeout setting
266: Confirm first that the PDP context is active and has an IP
267: Open a TLS connection (buffer mode, you read the data yourself)
268: Up to 150 s plus the negotiatetime setting (manual default 300 s)
269: This really goes online and completes a TLS handshake; the certificate chain alone is several KB, and the 1NCE prepaid SIM bills for it. The AT port can block for 150 s or more during the handshake (plus negotiatetime), so issue no other command meanwhile.
271: The remote server's domain name or IP. A domain name goes through DNS and returns error code 565 if resolution fails. The manual's example address 192.0.2.2 is a documentation-reserved address, not a real server.
272: The server's listening port. 443 for HTTPS, 8883 for MQTT over TLS. The manual's examples use 8010/8011.
273: Open a TLS connection (direct push, data comes straight out as URCs)
274: This really goes online, completes a TLS handshake and generates data traffic (billed on the 1NCE prepaid SIM). In direct push mode the module dumps received data straight onto the AT port, so a peer that keeps sending will flood the terminal.
275: The remote server's domain name or IP. The only difference from buffer mode is the last parameter <access_mode>=1: received data is emitted directly as URCs by the module and you never issue AT+QSSLRECV.
276: The server's listening port. 443 for HTTPS, 8883 for MQTT over TLS.
277: List the state of every SSL connection
280: Send data (two-stage: wait for > then send the body, no Ctrl+Z)
281: After the module replies >, it only sends once it has counted the exact number of bytes you declared. If the length is wrong or you abort midway, the AT port stays stuck in data mode and swallows every command that follows — this tool cannot send ESC (0x1B) to cancel, so the only ways out are closing the connection or restarting the module. The data really goes online and costs traffic.
283: The bytes actually sent. The length is counted in UTF-8 and filled into the command's <sendlen> automatically (a Chinese character counts as 3 bytes), limit 1460 bytes (manual §2.2.3). Note: this is a text input, so you cannot type control characters such as CR/LF — protocols that must end with \r\n\r\n, like an HTTP request, cannot be sent in full.

288: Close the connection (default wait up to 10 s)
290: Close the connection with an explicit timeout (0=immediate)
291: Determined by the <close_timeout> you enter, maximum 65535
293: Range 0–65535, manual default 10, 0=close immediately. The unit is set by AT+QSSLCFG="closetimemode" (0=seconds, 1=milliseconds). You must also run this after receiving +QSSLURC: "closed", otherwise the state stays at closing instead of returning to initial.

295: List every configurable item and its parameter range
296: Read back every current HTTP setting at once
297: Bind the PDP context HTTP will use

324: Query each PDP context's state and the IP it obtained

328: Set the PDP context's APN and authentication method

346: Must match exactly the number set with AT+QHTTPCFG="sslctxid", range 0–5
348: 0=SSL3.0, 1=TLS1.0, 2=TLS1.1, 3=TLS1.2, 4=All. The HTTP AN example uses 1 (TLS1.0), but that example is from 2020; modern servers mostly accept TLS1.2 only, so use 4
349: Set the cipher suite; 0XFFFF = support all
352: Hexadecimal. 0XFFFF = Support all cipher suites (the least trouble). The manual's example uses 0X0005 (TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA); RC4 is disabled on modern servers, so do not copy it
353: Certificate authentication level; in practice this tool can only use 0
355: 0=No authentication (the server certificate is not verified), 1=verify the server, 2=mutual verification. 1 needs a CA certificate in UFS and 2 also needs a client cert plus key; the manual's example uploads binary files with AT+QFUPL, which this tool cannot do, so only 0 works
356: Enable SNI; almost mandatory for HTTPS sites on a shared IP
357: 0=disabled, 1=enable Server Name Indication. HTTPS sites behind a CDN or virtual hosting (many domains on one IP) fail the handshake without it
358: Maximum TLS handshake wait in seconds
360: Range 10–300, default 300. A smaller value reports a failed handshake sooner instead of waiting out 5 minutes
361: Read back the currently configured URL (a plain query, not two-stage)
362: Two-stage: declare the length → wait for CONNECT → send the URL bytes
365: How many seconds the module waits for you to finish sending the URL, range 1–65535, default 60. On timeout with fewer bytes than <URL_length>, the module returns to command mode and emits +CME ERROR
367: Must start with http:// or https:// (that decides whether TLS is used). Do NOT append CR/LF when sending, or they count toward the length. Manual §3.1.1 example: AT+QHTTPURL=23,80 → CONNECT → HTTP://www.example.com/ → OK; that string is exactly 23 bytes, which proves there are no line-ending characters
368: Send GET; OK only means the command was accepted, and the result comes as a URC
370: This really connects to the server and fetches data, consuming 1NCE prepaid traffic directly. The <content_length> in the URC is the byte count of the response body, so make sure the URL points at a small file before pressing.
372: How many seconds to wait for the +QHTTPGET URC, range 1–65535, default 60. Note this is "how long after OK", not a timeout for the whole command
373: Fetch only the slice at the given offset and length, saving traffic
374: It still connects and consumes 1NCE traffic, but fetches only {rlen} bytes. Restrictions: it can only run while AT+QHTTPCFG="requestheader",0, and the server always answers with 206 (Partial Content).
377: Where the data you want begins (in bytes). The manual states no range
379: How many bytes to fetch this time. The manual states no range. Probe with a small value before pulling a big file to save traffic
380: Read the response; everything after CONNECT is raw bytes
381: Determined by {wait} (the maximum gap between two data packets, 1–65535 s, default 60)
382: Once it runs, the serial port enters data mode and any character sent meanwhile is treated as data. The real end marker is the final standalone line +QHTTPREAD: <err>, not the OK in the middle — the response body (HTML/JSON) can itself contain the words OK or CONNECT.
384: <wait_time>: the maximum gap in seconds between two received data packets, range 1–65535, default 60. It is not a total duration, so a slow large file is not cut short, but a stall longer than this returns a non-zero +QHTTPREAD. Note: the EG800K firmware on this unit accepts only this one parameter (AT+QHTTPREAD=? replies (1-65535)); the chunked <read_len> forms in the application note return a bare ERROR in practice, so do not copy them
385: Two-stage: wait for CONNECT, then send the body bytes
386: Determined by the network and {rsptime}; CONNECT itself can take up to 125 s
387: This really sends data and downloads the response, consuming 1NCE prepaid traffic. Two traps: (1) the manual says CONNECT appears "within 125 s" — the module first has to connect to the server and send the request header, so the prompt timeout must be set to 125 s and cannot reuse MQTT's 5 s; (2) {len} must equal the byte count of the body (or of header+body when requestheader=1) — get it wrong and you are stuck in data mode until {input_time} expires.
388: Maximum seconds to send the body, range 1–65535, default 60. A timeout with too few bytes returns +QHTTPPOST: <err> (not +CME ERROR)
389: Maximum seconds to wait for the +QHTTPPOST URC, range 1–65535, default 60
391: Sent as-is, with no CR/LF added. The manual §3.1.2.1 example AT+QHTTPPOST=20,80,80 corresponds to the body Message=HelloQuectel, exactly 20 bytes, which proves there are no line-ending characters. Content-Type comes from AT+QHTTPCFG="contenttype"
392: POST from a UFS file; this tool cannot upload the file first
393: This tool cannot upload files to the module's UFS, so this button is only meaningful when the file already exists (for example something saved earlier with AT+QHTTPREADFILE). It still connects and consumes traffic.
395: String type, file name up to 80 bytes. The manual's example uses "UFS:2.txt". With requestheader=0 the file content is used as the body only; with =1 the file must contain a complete header plus body
396: Save the response into a UFS file; this tool cannot read the file back
398: String type, file name up to 80 bytes. This command does not enter data mode (it returns OK and then waits for a URC), so it will not pollute the terminal — but that also means you cannot see the content; retrieving it needs the file AT commands, which are outside this tool's scope
399: Maximum gap in seconds between two data packets, 1–65535, default 60
400: Cancel the GET/POST in progress and drop the session
402: Deactivate the PDP context, closing every connection on it
403: 40 s (network dependent; other AT commands get no response meanwhile)
404: This closes every TCP/IP connection on that context and releases the IP; afterwards all HTTP commands fail and you must run AT+QIACT again to continue. PDP 1 on this unit is activated automatically, and there is no guarantee it comes back by itself after a manual deactivation. The manual also lists it as the rescue path for DNS/GET failures (QIDEACT, then QIACT).
406: Confirm first that the PDP context is active and has an IP; QFTPOPEN always fails without it
407: List every configurable item and its supported range; press this first for reference while developing
408: Choose which PDP context FTP uses; activate it with QIACT first
410: Range 1–15, default 1. It must be a context already activated with AT+QIACT, otherwise QFTPOPEN fails
411: Query the currently bound PDP context ID
412: Set the login credentials; this must be done before QFTPOPEN
413: String, up to 255 bytes. The manual's example uses test. The manual does not describe how to write an anonymous FTP username
414: String, up to 255 bytes. Note: the query command prints the password in clear text on the terminal
415: Query the current credentials (the password is shown in clear text on the terminal)
416: Transfer mode; FTPS always requires 1 (passive), and 1 is also recommended behind mobile-network NAT
418: 0=active mode (the module opens a port and waits for the server to connect in); 1=passive mode (the server opens a port for the module to dial out to). The manual states that FTPS does not support active mode, so it must be 1
419: Transfer data type; use 1 for plain text files and 0 for everything else
421: 0=Binary, 1=ASCII. This only affects the FTP transfer type (TYPE I / TYPE A); it will not turn binary content into readable characters
422: The maximum response time for most FTP commands, and also the maximum gap between two data packets in data mode
424: Range 20–180 s, default 90. For QFTPPUT/GET/LIST/NLST it caps the time from issuing the command to CONNECT; once in data mode it becomes the cap on the gap between two data packets
425: Set 0 for plain FTP; change it to 1 or 2 only for FTPS
427: 0=FTP client, 1=FTPS implicit encryption (the port is usually 990), 2=FTPS explicit encryption. With any non-zero value, transmode must be 1
428: Choose the SSL context; the detailed parameters are set separately with AT+QSSLCFG (not covered in this document)
430: Range 0–5, default 0. After setting it, use AT+QSSLCFG on the same id to set ciphersuite / seclevel / sslversion; see the SSL Application Note
431: Which address the data connection uses in passive mode; adjust this when it will not connect behind NAT
433: 0=use the address the server assigns; 1=use the control connection's address; 2=prefer the control connection's address and fall back to the server-assigned one (you may then add data_timeout, range 15–50 s, default 25)
434: Download cache size and mode; pick 2 if you need resume capability
436: 0=default mode, 64 KB cache; 1=fast mode, 128 KB cache; 2=slow mode, 128 KB cache with support to resume the download
437: How the data connection is closed; use 0 when the server is sensitive to RST
439: 0=normal wavehand close; 1=send an RST packet directly. The manual states no default
440: Query the current connection state; confirm it is 1 (open and idle) before acting
442: Log in to the FTP(S) server; OK only means the command was accepted, and the URC decides whether the login succeeded
444: This opens an outbound connection and starts consuming mobile data (1NCE prepaid SIM). The command can block for up to 125 s before answering, so do not hammer other FTP commands meanwhile.
446: IP or domain name, up to 255 bytes. With a domain name, +QFTPOPEN: 604,0 means DNS resolution failed
448: Range 1–65535, default 21. The FTPS port is decided by the server provider; the manual says it is usually 990
450: Query the current working directory on the server
451: Change the working directory; every later file and directory operation is relative to it
453: String, up to 128 bytes. The root directory is "/". The manual does not define the behavior of relative paths such as ..
454: List the current directory in full, dumping the data straight to the terminal (omitting the parameter defaults to COM:)
455: It emits CONNECT and enters data mode; the directory listing is printed as raw bytes and any character you send meanwhile is treated as data. It also consumes mobile data.
456: List a specified directory in full, dumped straight to the terminal
457: Enters data mode and consumes mobile data.
459: String, up to 255 bytes. "." means the current directory set by QFTPCWD. local_name is hard-coded to "COM:" (max 60 bytes); change it to UFS:/SD: and the data goes into the module's file system where this tool cannot read it
460: List file names only (no size or permissions), cheaper in traffic than LIST
461: List file and directory information in the standard MLSD format, easier to parse than LIST
462: Query a file's modification time without downloading its content
464: Check the file size before downloading, so a whole-file download does not blow your data budget
465: String, up to 255 bytes. Returns +QFTPSIZE: 0,<file_size> in bytes
466: Chunked download to the terminal; the download method this tool recommends most
467: Consumes mobile data and enters data mode (CONNECT → raw bytes → OK). If the file is not plain text, the terminal shows garbage.
470: Which byte of the file to start at, default 0. For the next chunk, use the previous chunk's startpos+transferlen
472: How many bytes to emit this time; only effective when local_name is "COM:". The module leaves data mode once it has emitted that many. A reported transferlen smaller than this value means the whole file has been transferred
473: Download the whole file straight to the terminal, no chunking
474: Per rsptimeout (default 90 s, meaning the maximum gap between two data packets)
475: Whole-file download: a large file eats a lot of 1NCE prepaid data at once and ties up the terminal for a long time. Always check the size with AT+QFTPSIZE first, and use the chunked version for large files.
476: String, up to 255 bytes. Omitting startpos and downloadlen downloads the whole file
477: Query how many bytes the last PUT/GET/LIST/NLST actually transferred
478: Escape from data mode back to AT mode; it must be sent as raw bytes with no CR/LF
479: This button cannot use the normal command path (no line ending may be appended) and must go through the raw byte channel. The manual requires at least 1 s of silence before sending, all three + within 1 s, and no further character for 1 s afterwards, otherwise they are treated as data.
480: Re-enter data mode to keep receiving data that was not finished
481: ATO can only take you back to data mode after QFTPGET / QFTPLIST / QFTPNLST — not after QFTPPUT.
482: Upload plain text pasted from the terminal; the module leaves data mode automatically once len bytes have been sent
483: This writes to the remote server and consumes uplink data. After CONNECT you must send exactly len bytes as raw bytes, with no CR/LF appended. This tool cannot read binary files, so plain text only.
484: The file name on the server after upload, up to 255 bytes
485: The bytes actually sent; the length is counted in UTF-8 and filled into the command automatically (a Chinese character counts as 3 bytes). No line ending is appended.
487: Create a folder in the server's current directory
489: Rename a file or folder on the server
492: Delete a file on the server
493: Deletes the file on the remote server outright. It cannot be undone.
494: Delete a folder on the server
495: Deletes the folder on the remote server outright. It cannot be undone.
496: Log out of the FTP(S) server; once the URC arrives you can QFTPOPEN again
497: Deactivate the PDP context; press it only when you want a full network reset
498: This drops the whole PDP connection, and every other function on the module that depends on this context (MQTT / HTTP / TCP) goes down with it; you must run AT+QIACT=1 again to reconnect.
499: The PDP context ID to deactivate, usually 1
